questions.q: According to this lesson, how should Chapters 7 through 10 be understood together?
options: As four alternative strategies where only one should actually be used
As four parts of one ongoing job: know what's happening, keep it healthy, fix what's slow, and automate watching it
As a strict sequence that only applies once, not an ongoing practice
As four completely unrelated, independent DBA responsibilities
questions.explain: Monitoring, performance tuning, maintenance, and automation are framed as one continuous responsibility, not separate silos.

questions.q: Why does index maintenance belong on a SCHEDULE rather than an always-on alert?
options: Index maintenance should never run at all in a real strategy
It's a routine health task that doesn't need instant reaction — putting it on an alert instead would be unnecessary complexity
Scheduled tasks and always-on alerts are exactly the same mechanism
Index maintenance can only ever run as an always-on alert
questions.explain: The real distinction is reaction speed needed — fragmentation building up over time doesn't need a second-by-second alert.

questions.q: What real operational risk does putting CPU monitoring on a 15-minute schedule instead of an always-on alert create?
options: Scheduled CPU monitoring is actually faster to react than an alert
A real problem can sit unnoticed for up to 15 minutes before anyone or anything reacts to it
CPU issues resolve themselves automatically regardless of monitoring approach
There is no real risk — scheduled and always-on monitoring are functionally identical
questions.explain: Always-on alerting exists specifically to close that reaction-time gap for time-sensitive conditions.

questions.q: In the example strategy, what is reviewed weekly BY A HUMAN, rather than automated?
options: CPU and storage alerts, which require manual checking every 15 minutes
DBCC CHECKDB, which only a human can ever run
Query Store's top resource consumers and job history for any silent failures
Nothing — the entire strategy in this lesson is fully automated with no human review
questions.explain: The strategy deliberately keeps a human reviewing trends and confirming alerts caught what they should have, rather than staring at a live dashboard.

questions.q: What comes immediately after Chapter 10, and what's the real shift in focus?
options: Chapter 11 repeats SQL Server Agent content from Chapter 10
Chapter 11, Azure Automation & Infrastructure as Code — moving from Agent-based automation to Azure-native automation (CLI, PowerShell, IaC)
Chapter 11 returns to basic T-SQL syntax review
The course ends after Chapter 10
questions.explain: Chapter 11 shifts from the Agent-centric automation of Chapter 10 toward Azure's own automation tooling.
